content: The Ernest Orlando Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL) is a national laboratory under the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) that focuses on unclassified scientific research. It is situated on the University of California, Berkeley campus, specifically in the Berkeley Hills above the central campus. The laboratory is managed and operated by the University of California and holds the distinction of being the oldest national laboratory within the DOE system. The laboratory was originally established on August 26, 1931, as the Radiation Laboratory of the University of California. It was founded by Ernest Orlando Lawrence, a physicist who developed the cyclotron, a groundbreaking particle accelerator. Lawrence was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1939 for this invention. During the 1930s, Lawrence worked to build increasingly larger cyclotrons to advance physics research. He often sought funding from private philanthropists, promising potential medical applications such as new forms of chemotherapy using radioisotopes produced by the cyclotrons. After missing out on several key discoveries, the laboratory began collaborating more closely with theoretical physicists at Berkeley, including Robert Oppenheimer. In 1940, the laboratory relocated to its current site in the Berkeley Hills because its machines, particularly the 184-inch cyclotron, had grown too large and potentially hazardous to remain on the university campus. During World War II, Lawrence secured government sponsorship for the laboratory as part of the Manhattan Project, the U.S. effort to develop the atomic bomb. The 184-inch cyclotron was repurposed as a mass spectrometer, leading to the development of electromagnetic uranium enrichment techniques. These techniques were later used in the calutrons at the Y-12 facility in Oak Ridge, Tennessee, contributing to the production of fissile material for the Little Boy bomb dropped on Hiroshima. After the war, Lawrence worked to maintain strong ties between the laboratory and the government, integrating it into the newly established Atomic Energy Commission (now the DOE) system of national laboratories. By the early 1950s, the laboratory shifted its focus primarily to non-classified research, with classified weapons research being conducted at Los Alamos National Laboratory and the newly established Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory. However, some weapons-related research continued at LBNL until the 1970s. Following Lawrence's death in 1959, the laboratory was renamed the Ernest O. Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory, though it was often referred to as the Rad Lab or LBL. Over time, the name Berkeley Lab also became widely used. Since the 1950s, the laboratory has expanded its research scope beyond physics to include astrophysics, nuclear fusion, earth sciences, genomics, health physics, computer science, materials science, and environmental science. It is home to several National User Facilities, such as the Advanced Light Source, the National Center for Electron Microscopy, the National Energy Research Scientific Computing Center, the Energy Sciences Network, and the Molecular Foundry. The laboratory spans 76 buildings on 200 acres in the Berkeley Hills, with the land owned by the University of California and the buildings owned by the DOE. It employs approximately 4,000 people, including 800 students, and hosts over 3,000 visiting researchers annually. Around two dozen DOE employees are stationed at the lab to oversee its operations. The laboratory is organized into 17 scientific divisions, covering areas such as Computing Sciences, Physical Sciences, Life and Environmental Sciences, and General Sciences. Many research projects involve collaboration across multiple divisions, with computational and engineering expertise integrated into biosciences, general sciences, and energy sciences. The laboratory director, appointed by the Regents of the University of California, reports to the university's president. The current director is Steve Chu. Although LBNL operates independently of the UC Berkeley campus, the two institutions maintain close ties. Over 200 LBNL researchers hold joint appointments as Berkeley faculty, and more than 500 Berkeley graduate students conduct research at the lab. LBNL is also a partner in the Joint Genome Institute, founded in 1997 to advance genome mapping, DNA sequencing, and related technologies. Additionally, the laboratory manages the DOE's high-speed research network, ESnet. Since World War II, LBNL has achieved numerous scientific milestones, including the observation of the antiproton, the discovery of several transuranic elements, and the confirmation of the accelerating expansion of the universe. Eleven researchers affiliated with the lab have received Nobel Prizes, including Ernest Lawrence, Glenn T. Seaborg, Edwin M. McMillan, Owen Chamberlain, Emilio G. Segrè, Donald A. Glaser, Melvin Calvin, Luis W. Alvarez, Yuan T. Lee, Steve Chu, and George F. Smoot. Elements discovered at the lab include astatine, neptunium, plutonium, curium, americium, berkelium, californium, einsteinium, fermium, mendelevium, nobelium, lawrencium, dubnium, and seaborgium. Some of these elements are named after the laboratory or its scientists. The lab also contributed to the development of networking tools such as libpcap, tcpdump, and traceroute. However, the laboratory has faced controversies, including a major scandal in 2002 involving Victor Ninov, a researcher who fabricated evidence for the creation of elements ununoctium and ununhexium. This led to the retraction of two scientific articles and became one of the most significant scandals in physics.
